name: Probabilistic Logic Network (PLN)
analogy: Think of it as a case file where every claim carries two stamps: how likely it is, and how much evidence is behind that. A claim backed by two cases and one backed by two thousand can share the same odds, yet they are not trusted equally.

steps.title: Write each fact with two numbers
steps.description: Every statement in the knowledge base carries a strength, which is how likely it is, and a confidence, which is how much evidence supports that strength. Keeping the two apart is the core idea of the model.
steps.inExample: A volume spike is followed by a breakout with strength 62 percent and confidence 70 percent, because 140 past cases back it.

steps.title: Link facts into chains of if-then
steps.description: Statements are joined by links such as if this then that. A link inherits its strength and confidence from the evidence behind it, so the knowledge base is a web of uncertain implications.
steps.inExample: A second link says a news release is followed by a volume spike with strength 80 percent and confidence 50 percent.

steps.title: Chain links by deduction
steps.description: If one link leads from A to B and another from B to C, a new link from A to C is derived. Its strength is roughly the product of the two strengths, and its confidence is lower than either, because each indirect step adds doubt.
steps.inExample: News release to breakout is derived with strength about 50 percent and confidence about 35 percent.

steps.title: Derive other directions with induction and abduction
steps.description: From observed cases the model can generalize forward (induction) or infer a likely cause backward (abduction). Each pattern has its own formula for combining the premises into a conclusion, always carrying a confidence with it.
steps.inExample: Seeing a breakout after a volume spike suggests news may be the cause, supported with low confidence.

steps.title: Merge independent sources by revision
steps.description: When two sources give separate estimates of the same statement, they are combined weighted by their confidences, so the better-supported estimate counts for more. The merged confidence is higher than either source alone.
steps.inExample: Direct evidence of 22 cases says news release to breakout is 45 percent at confidence 30 percent; merging with the derived 50 percent at 35 percent gives about 48 percent at 50 percent.

steps.title: Report the conclusion with its trace
steps.description: The result is a strength-and-confidence pair plus the chain of rules that produced it, so a reader can see how the confidence was built and where it was eroded.
steps.inExample: The trace shows one derived link and one direct source merged, ending at strength 48 percent and confidence 50 percent.

useFor.example: Labelling each hand-written MNQ rule with how likely it works and how many cases back that claim, so a rule seen twice is not treated like one seen 2,000 times.

useFor.task: Deriving a belief with no direct data
useFor.example: Estimating the breakout odds after a rare news event by chaining two well-tested implications.
Combining a technical rule, a FinBERT sentiment rule and an ES correlation rule into one strength-and-confidence pair.
Showing the chain of rules behind a trade idea, with the confidence at each link.

avoidWhen: You have a large table of labelled bars and just want a prediction; a supervised model learns directly from the table, while this model needs hand-built rules.
You need the model to be tuned and tested by standard cross-validation, since this style of reasoning does not have a mature tooling for fold-based evaluation.

example.scenario: A research desk has two rules on file about MNQ and wants a belief about how often a scheduled news release is followed by a breakout, a case it has only seen 22 times.

input.summary: Three pieces of evidence, each with a strength and a confidence.

fields.name: volume spike then breakout: strength
fields.meaning: How often a breakout of the prior 12-bar range followed a volume spike of more than 50 percent above average.

fields.name: volume spike then breakout: confidence
fields.meaning: How well supported that strength is; 140 past cases stand behind it.

fields.name: news release then volume spike: strength
fields.meaning: How often a scheduled release was followed by a volume spike.

fields.name: news release then volume spike: confidence
fields.meaning: How well supported that strength is, from a smaller set of cases.

fields.name: direct cases of news then breakout
fields.meaning: A separate, directly observed estimate whose confidence is only 30 percent because it is a small count.

output.summary: A merged belief about news release followed by breakout, with the chain that built it.

fields.name: derived strength and confidence
fields.meaning: The result of chaining the two rules; the confidence is lower than either rule's.

fields.name: merged strength
fields.meaning: The derived and direct estimates combined, weighted by their confidences.

fields.name: merged confidence
fields.meaning: How well supported the merged strength is, higher than either source alone.

example.reading: A strength of 48 percent at 50 percent confidence says roughly even odds with only moderate backing, which is the honest answer for a rare event. Use it to decide how much to trust the rule, and let further cases lift the confidence before the rule is allowed to move real position size.
